title: Constant-competitive online matching on the line
formal: Historical question, resolved negatively: does there exist a deterministic online algorithm and an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every \(k\ge1\), every known set of \(k\) server positions on the real line and every sequence of \(k\) arriving client positions, immediate irrevocable matching to unused servers costs at most \(C\) times the optimal offline matching cost?

source_formulation.text: It is still an open question whether constant-competitive algorithms exist for OMM-Line.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

why: The negative answer establishes that even one-dimensional geometry cannot give a universal constant cost guarantee for irrevocable online matching.
status_note: Resolved negatively by the published ICALP 2021 theorem. The source model and theorem were checked on 13 September 2026; this is a theorem-to-model match, not an independent proof audit or a Lean certificate.

progress.text: The source records the constant-competitiveness question.
The ICALP theorem proves an \(\Omega(\sqrt{\log k})\) competitive-ratio lower bound, resolving the historical question negatively.

category_assignment.reason: Irrevocable choices or bounded recourse under arriving requests determine the guarantee, including online packing, coloring, matching and spanners.

importance.reason: A fundamental historical competitiveness question in the simplest nontrivial metric, now settled by a general lower bound.

sentences: The historical question asks for a constant competitive ratio when clients must be matched immediately to known servers on a line.
Earlier assignments cannot be changed and all matched distances contribute to cost.
The comparison is with an optimal matching that knows the full request sequence.
A 2021 lower bound grows with the number of servers and applies even to randomized algorithms.
Consequently the deterministic constant-competitive target is resolved negatively.

context_blocks.text: The 2020 source asks whether a constant competitive ratio is possible without reassigning earlier clients.

Peserico and Scquizzato subsequently proved an \(\Omega(\sqrt{\log k})\) lower bound for arbitrary randomized online algorithms on the line. This also rules out the deterministic strategy asked for here. Their inputs use a known server set and an obliviously generated request sequence.

source_consolidations.note: Both introductory passages concern irrevocable bipartite matching of arriving clients to a known set of servers on the line, with sum of distances as cost and worst-case arrival order. Their deterministic O(log k) benchmark and deterministic constant-lower-bound discussion support the deterministic constant-competitive question. Randomized algorithms against oblivious adversaries form a distinct variant; the general-metric randomized discussion and recourse results are not substituted for a deterministic no-recourse guarantee.

definitions: Servers are individually labeled and their positions are known before requests arrive. Client positions are revealed one at a time; the algorithm must match each to one unused server before seeing the next. Positions may coincide. An assignment cannot later be changed. Cost is the sum of absolute differences of matched positions. The offline optimum sees the complete client sequence and uses each server once. The inequality is required even when that optimum is zero. C is independent of k, coordinates and arrival order; there is no additive term. The model measures matching cost with no restriction on internal computation. The algorithm is deterministic, so worst-case fixed sequences and adaptively chosen sequences yield the same universal guarantee. No randomness, random-order promise or recourse is allowed.
answer_criterion: The published answer is NO. A Lean certificate of this answer would prove that every deterministic online strategy and every finite \(C\) fail on some finite server configuration and arrival sequence. The cited randomized lower bound implies this negation; no Lean formalization is supplied by this editorial review.
